title: Can a solo dev build a Deponia-scale point-and-click in 12 months? My journey from SD 1.5 to MiniMax H3
author: novokvest
selftext:
Think about your favorite cult classic point-and-click adventure games. From LucasArts masterpieces to Daedalic's modern hits, they have almost always been the product of fully staffed, professional animation and design studios.

My own love for this genre started early. The very first game I ever played on my PC was *The Neverhood*, followed quickly by an obsession with Humongous Entertainment classics like *Freddi Fish* in the 90s. As I grew older, I played almost all the classics, but Daedalic's *Chaos on Deponia* remains my absolute favorite point-and-click adventure of all time.

What I love about this genre is the core design philosophy: you play completely at your own pace, solve logic puzzles, and explore beautifully expressive cartoon worlds. Unlike visual novels, you actually feel like you are *playing* a game.

As a software developer, I always harbored a dream of making video games. But I never seriously considered building a point-and-click adventure. The genre is historically a production black hole. To match the scale of a professional game like *Deponia*—which features an 8-to-10 hour runtime, 50+ unique, beautifully detailed background slates, and thousands of custom frames for character animations and walk cycles—it would take an eternity for a single person. Even a shorter, stylized *Freddi Fish* kind of game requires a mountain of manual asset illustration, frame rigging, and voice lines.

That all changed for me in 2022.

**2022: The Local GPU Realization (The SD 1.5 Era)**

I remember running vanilla Stable Diffusion 1.5 locally on my old GTX 1080Ti. The images it spat out back then were objectively terrible—but they were *weirdly* terrible. They had an uncanny, accidental style to them. Crucially, they were still vastly better than anything I could draw with a mouse in MS Paint.

That was the exact moment I realized: *I can actually make a point-and-click adventure game.* I immediately had an idea for a narrative about a character stuck in a dream who has to decipher the dream's logic to wake up.

[Alien Bazaar concept](https://preview.redd.it/308zm21d7erh1.png?width=960&format=png&auto=webp&s=07c1b08036b8b0dd1f261547b8ee933afec1a4ed)

**2023: Turning the Corner (Godot, Escoria, and Civitai)**

By 2023, the open-source pipeline exploded. Community merges like *Dreamshaper* and *Deliberate* dropped on Civitai, alongside early ControlNets. Suddenly, keeping characters consistent and generating structured backgrounds became possible. I learned a trick to generate full character turnaround sheets in a single prompt and built my first functional point-and-click demo using **Godot 3** and the **Escoria framework**.

[Flight Attendant](https://preview.redd.it/paty901g9erh1.jpg?width=1533&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=1416b7e1e3f623a564b0ca1381c033af6fbc01c1)

But I hit a massive wall: **walking animations**.

The only workflow that worked back then was a grueling 3D-to-2D bypass. I had to learn a bit of Blender (yes, I made the mandatory donut), find video game character walk cycles, record them, and feed them into ControlNets and early AnimateDiff workflows. It looked okay, but requiring full 3D modeling and animation just to get a 2D sprite to walk completely killed the "solo dev speed" I was aiming for.

**2025: Image to video**

Everything changed again when **Wan 2.1** dropped. For the first time, we had a video model where you could prompt a flawless walking animation starting directly from a single 2D character frame. Getting them to loop smoothly was a nightmare at first, but it was an absolute game-changer. Coupled with incredible open-source text-to-speech tools and a beefier RTX 3090, I finally built my first demo that felt more like an actual game.

[Escoria 2077](https://preview.redd.it/kvr90f2laerh1.jpg?width=1920&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=b786601a4ae077207df6b38bd0a8959f514f4063)

Shortly after, first-and-last-frame support arrived in the video generation ecosystem, making perfect 2D walking cycles an easily repeatable problem. You just feed the exact same frame as both the first and last frame.

[Wan 2.2 first last frame](https://i.redd.it/jpqpwqvhcerh1.gif)

**2026: Video with sounds** **(LTX 2.3 to MiniMax H3)**

With the arrival of open-weights models like **LTX 2.3**, the architecture evolved to generate videos natively embedded with sounds. This has completely transformed how I handle game development: it is currently the best way to auto-generate organic environmental SFX or pull clean, initial voice samples for TTS voice cloning pipelines.

To put this modern workflow to the test, I entered the recent AI Game Jam and built a short adventure called ***The Princess and the Mech***. Using a strict prompt-to-asset pipeline, I built a playable game featuring **7 interactive rooms in just 18 days**.

The jam results were mixed. While the game managed to place **5th in Graphics**, it only scored **52nd in Fun**. It was the perfect proof of a major reality check: AI graphics won't carry a weak game loop.

[The Princess and the Mech](https://preview.redd.it/7u54ksd3ferh1.jpg?width=1920&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=c33f8f5b2ef15abb40ccc2b1ec8b379f5fec5b66)

Since finishing the jam, I’ve been toying with the new local **MiniMax H3** model, and it is a massive generational leap—outperforming both LTX 2.3 and Wan 2.2 in almost every visual and physical aspect.

  
**The Verdict: Is a solo "Deponia" possible in a year?**

Absolutely. With current high-fidelity image foundation models like **Krea 2** for art direction control and video/audio generation like **MiniMax** to handle environmental motion and spatial sounds, a single developer can generate the environmental scope of a studio in a matter of months.

But my jam data proves that shiny assets won't save a rushed game. The time we save on drawing must be 100% reinvested into what actually makes a point-and-click great: the writing, the puzzle choreography, and the human author's voice. The tech handles the manual labor of painting 50 rooms so that we can finally focus on being storytellers.

replies.author: sw3d
replies.body: The character and walking animation is really nice. Wish there was running/more to it. The vibe shifts quickly between scenes (music and visuals) which is something to watch out for with AI, it all looks good in isolation but it takes away from the immersion

replies.author: novokvest
replies.body: Thanks a lot for checking out! Yeah, it is super important for a real game.

comments.author: Droooomp
comments.body:
Yep yep you are on the right track, i am trying to do 2 sec loops with h3,  started working on something, in godot, personally I am focusing highly on the animation system. If i manage to do 2 sec loops would be great for inbetweens. for bg removal i vibecoded an app that uses either LiteSDMatte or BiRefNet both did well in different contexts, biref manages to work the best if i do 1024x1024 generations with h3 lower res is bad on bg removal needs manually erasing each frame after that. I use nanobanana for frames tho, start end frames for inbetweens and same frame for loops really nifty that it works so well for that. 

(i run it on a 4070ti takes about 5-10 min /10 sec usually i leave it overnight with a batch of 30 animations and prompt it with claude, surprisingly works better on micromovements than the qwen base enhancer) 

https://reddit.com/link/pbt9hxc/video/dc7602mlairh1/player

replies.author: novokvest
replies.body: That game looks nice! I like how you have animation transitions, like turning. In escoria there is no such system. Is it vanilla godot? Do you have global puzzle state management? Are you planning to make a whole point and click adventure game?

replies.author: Droooomp
replies.body:
Yes vanilla godot, i am not at the point of doing the puzzles, still working on the core systems and animations. Thats the plan to make it into a full game. I was wondering about the global or local stuff, gobliins was a good game at his time and they had local states.
For now i am working on the demo, 3 scenes with 4 characters.

replies.author: novokvest
replies.body: Well, the game looks great so far, I hope it would be a whole story! It looks like a classic fairy tale. Local state adventures are rare, we had a game in the 90s called Pilot Brothers that was insprired by Goblins and it felt awesome, check it out if you are not aware of it.

replies.author: Droooomp
replies.body:
Thank you, when i have the demo i will put it on itch, see what the reactions are if all goes well i will continue.

Its a balkan fairytale mixed with some hero motifs, original story inspired from folklore. I am working on layering new stuff over the classics, it will be a shame not to take advantage of ai to push the systems to their max :)), i will check Pilot Brothers out.
